p: On Tuesday, March 9, Dot was found dead in an armchair at the Brown Palace hotel, holding Henry's card, with tea for two and one clean cup.

Her red folder says the capstone failed, her name for dual authorization, the rule that two people approve every big payment. Exception noted, see 1994. Her sticky note says check the year, and don't trust the dome.
The same morning London gave Henry a 300 million dollar cyber claim from Meridian Clearing, the payments company she used to examine. He told his boss he knew her, in writing, within the hour.
Nearly three thousand of the payments Meridian calls fraud sit just under ten thousand dollars, the line where a second approver has to look.
And late that night he found that Dot's old examiner login had signed in to Meridian at 3:12 in the morning, after she died.
The waitress. She's served Henry and Dot at the diner on Colfax every Saturday since June.
Giles Fenwick. Henry's claims director in London. He wants a view by Friday.
Maisie Ashby. Henry's daughter. Her science fair project is on Benford's law, how to catch made up numbers.
Priyanka. Henry's colleague at Vellacott in London. Brisk, and usually right.
Laura. Maisie's mother, and Henry's ex wife.

At ten to three on Wednesday morning Henry did the thing his daughter had told him about by text. He took the first digit of every settlement on Meridian's list, all twelve thousand four hundred of them, and counted how many began with a 1, how many with a 2, and so on up to 9. It took one short query in the free database tool on his laptop and about four seconds. He didn't write the query down. He was tired, and it was only four seconds.
Meridian claim list, settlements by first digit (Henry's first run, 2:52 AM). If the amounts were ordinary, the bars should fall away from left to right, with 1 the tallest and 9 the shortest.
The bars fell away nicely from 1 to 8, the way Maisie said real numbers did. Then the last one stood up like a man who'd been called on in class.

At seven he went to the diner on Colfax, because it was where he went when he needed to think, and because he hadn't yet worked out where else to go. It was a Wednesday, so the booth by the window was empty for the ordinary reason. The waitress who'd served them every Saturday since June came over with the pot and two mugs, set both down, and then looked at the empty side of the booth.

He told her. She stood there with the pot for a while. Then she picked up the second mug, carried it as far as the counter, stopped, came back, and put it down again where it had been, upside down. On the house, she said, which made no sense, and he understood it completely.

He propped the chart against the ketchup bottle, where Dot would have read it upside down, faster than he could right way up. There was a bowl of sugar packets by the window. He took one and tore it into thin strips and laid them side by side, and then sat looking at them, because it turned out he didn't know what she'd been listening for.

The tall bar was still there when he looked back at it. Three thousand three hundred and forty settlements began with a 9. He didn't know yet what that meant. He knew a fourteen year old in Boulder who would.

By twenty past eight the chart was on the whiteboard in the Wazee Street office, under the order of work, the shopping list, and a line in his own capitals: THURS 6, BOULDER. Henry worked out what the law said should be there. Benford's share for a 9, just under four point six percent, came to 567 of the 12,400. Meridian's list had 3,340.
He knew one more thing already. On Tuesday night he'd counted 2,906 settlements between $9,000 and $9,999, just under the line where a second person had to look. Every one of them began with a 9.
He had a lot of feelings about the bar. Dot would have asked him which of them were evidence.

He writes it as Dot taught him: what he observed, the expected number, the actual number, and what it might mean, in that order. Then a list of what could explain it. Amounts chosen to stay under the line. Ordinary business that happens to cluster there. A mistake in his own count. Each one gets a test beside it. The last one he almost doesn't write, and then does.

Data analytics finds patterns. Your job is to treat a pattern as a question and design the work that answers it, including the dull possibility that you got it wrong. That's professional skepticism pointed in both directions.

At 9:40 Meridian's broker sent a PDF with a cover note that said This should settle the controls question. It was a SOC 1 Type 1 report on Meridian's settlement services, issued by Hollins and Pike LLP, an outside audit firm.

Independent service auditor's report (extract). Report on the description of Meridian Clearing's settlement system and the suitability of the design of its controls, as of December 31, 2026. Opinion: the controls were suitably designed as of that date. Control 4.2: Settlement files above $10,000 require approval by a second authorized user.
Henry read the date three times, which was becoming a habit.

Design only, as of December 31. No testing of operation, nothing after that date, and the file says so plainly. He asks the broker for any Type 2 report covering 2026, the bridge letter to March, and the list of controls Meridian's customers are expected to run themselves. The broker replies within the hour. There's no Type 2. Meridian moved to the Type 1 last year.

Read the type, the period, and the scope. A Type 2 covers design and operating effectiveness over a period, which is what you need to rely on a control working. A bridge letter covers the gap to now. And going from Type 2 to Type 1 is worth noticing.
Giles rang at 10:30, which was half past five in London, and he sounded as if he'd walked to the phone from somewhere quite far away.

Idea, he said. Compliance has a questionnaire. Two hundred questions on controls. We send it to Meridian, they fill it in, you review the answers. Saves you days. Their internal audit chap's already offered to coordinate.

Happy to send it, he says. It'll tell me where they think they're strong. Then I test the ones that matter for the claim, starting with the reconciliations. Giles accepts this in the tone of a man who wanted to hear days saved and heard hours. Fine. And Leonard? Leonard can answer it. He shouldn't coordinate it.

Control self assessment helps people who own controls think about them, and it can point you at weak spots. It doesn't replace independent testing. Use it as an input to scoping, and keep the testing yours.

The list of 12,400 was Meridian's choice of rows. Henry wanted the rows they hadn't chosen: every settlement from March 2 to March 5, fraudulent or not, so he could see whether the list was complete and whether the strange 9s showed up anywhere else.
Meridian's general counsel answered his request at 11:15, copied to the broker, friendly and quick.

An email from Office of General Counsel, Meridian Clearing. Subject: Settlement data. Happy to help. Two options. Our database team can pull whatever you need into a spreadsheet today. Or, if you'd rather look yourself, we can set you up with a read only login to the settlement database by this afternoon.

The request takes five lines: every settlement record dated March 2 to 5, all fields except card and account numbers, the exact query used, the date and time it ran and by whom, and the system's own record count and dollar totals for those days. Through Vellacott's counsel, in writing. Counsel says tomorrow morning. Henry says that's fine, and it is.
Get data in a way you can stand behind. The query and run details show how it was produced. Control totals prove it's complete, and sending it through counsel keeps it usable as evidence.

At 1:40 Vellacott's counsel forwarded a short note from Agent Obi. The FBI had sent Meridian a preservation letter that morning for the examiner portal logs. Somewhere across town, a dead woman's sign in at 3:12 AM now had a case number, and Meridian still didn't know who'd found it.
At 2:05 he found the last tab of the claim spreadsheet, the one marked NOTES, which held three sentences.

Claim spreadsheet, tab NOTES. Fraud indicator set by Database Administration on March 6, 2027, using criteria agreed with Internal Audit. Rows with indicator Y are included in the claim. Prepared by L. Pratt.

So somebody with administrator rights to the settlement database had gone through the table on the Saturday after the event and marked which payments were fraud. Every dollar of the 41 million rested on those marks.

He adds it to the request through counsel: the database audit trail for the fraud indicator field, every change, by which account, and when, plus whatever shows that someone outside the DBA team reviewed it. Then he writes in his notes: 41M rests on flags set by privileged users. Change record and review requested.
The DBA can change data directly. The controls that matter are logging that activity and having somebody independent of the DBAs review it. Without both, the flags are just assertions in a column.
At 4:10 his phone buzzed. ok so you can see my project if you want. dont fix anything. Then a photo of a poster on a kitchen table, half finished, and a second text. the 3rd one is broken

The poster was called Who Made These Up? It had three charts. The first was the population of every town and city in Colorado, and its bars fell away from 1 to 9 like a staircase. The second was ten made up numbers each from thirty one people in her class, and its bars were nearly flat. The third was her mom's electric bills for the last four years, forty eight of them, every one between $61 and $148, and its bars made no sense at all.
He rang. It doesn't work, she said, before he'd said hello. The bills are real. They're totally real. And they don't follow it, so either Benford's wrong or I am.

What's the smallest bill, and what's the biggest? Smallest is sixty one. Biggest is a hundred forty eight. He doesn't say anything. Wait. That's not even triple. And my towns go from basically a gas station up to Denver. He keeps quiet, and hears her breathing change the way it used to when she was six and had nearly finished a jigsaw. When she speaks again it's very quiet. Oh my god. It's not broken. It just doesn't have room. She talks for ten minutes after that, fast, about orders of magnitude, and he mostly listens, which he notices is the first time in about a year she's needed him to.

Benford's law works on data that spans several orders of magnitude. Four years of household bills don't. One open question let her find the condition herself, which is how people actually learn when a test applies.

At half past seven, with noodles again, he started on the sample. Whatever Meridian's data said, sooner or later he'd have to take individual settlements back to their source: the settlement instruction, the merchant on the other end, the approval record. That meant choosing which ones.
Some rows practically volunteered. Settlements of $9,990, $9,995, and $9,999.00, sent at three in the morning, one after another, to the same handful of accounts. He could see the case making itself.

Two strata: the 2,906 between $9,000 and $9,999.99, and the other 9,494. Random selection within each, sized from a confidence level and tolerable error he writes down before he looks, with the seed beside them. Forty from the first group, sixty from the second. Then he writes the part he'd have skipped a year ago: how the sample was chosen and why, so somebody else could pick exactly the same rows.

Stratification splits a population into groups that behave differently and samples each, so a small important group gets proper coverage. Random selection lets you project, and writing down the method, size, and seed lets someone else re-perform it.
At ten past nine he found he'd written two questions at the top of the same page, and they weren't the same kind of question.

One was about the control. Through 2026, did a second approver actually sign off every settlement file over $10,000, the way the SOC report said the control was designed? The other was about the money. Of the 41 million, how much was really fraud? Dot's folder said the key control had failed years ago. The first question was the one that could prove her right.

The attribute is simple: a second approver's sign off, present or missing. He sets a tolerable deviation rate and a confidence level before he sees a single file, so the result can't move the goalposts. The variable sample for the dollars goes on a separate page. Two questions, two methods. Dot drew a line between them on a placemat once, with a sugar packet.

A compliance test of a control uses attribute sampling, which estimates the rate of deviation. Setting the tolerable rate in advance is what makes the result meaningful. Dollar questions get variable sampling separately.
At 10:40 he sent Maisie a photo of his chart, because she'd shown him hers.
The answer came back in four minutes.
A text from Maisie. ur bars add up to 12401 not 12400. which one is extra

He added them up. She was right. He opened the spreadsheet, scrolled to the bottom, and found it: the total row, $41,000,000, which began with a 4, sitting in his count like a passenger who'd got on without a ticket. The bar for 4 should have said 913.

He writes it under the chart: first run included the total row, counted 12,401, corrected to 12,400 at 10:52 PM, fours 914 to 913, conclusion unchanged, found by M. Ashby. Then he adds a step at the top of his own method: reconcile the row count before analysis. He texts back you're right. it was the total line. it's in my notes with your name on it. ur welcome, she sends, and then, a minute later, can i put that on my poster.

When you find an error in your own work, correct it openly: what was wrong, what changed, when, and the effect on the conclusion. Then fix the process that let it happen. Credit belongs to whoever found it.

On Thursday at half past seven he had a workpaper, a corrected chart, a sampling plan, and a Friday interim view due to Giles in a little over twenty four hours. He also had nobody who had checked any of it except a fourteen year old.
He'd always worked alone. It had always seemed efficient. At 7:31 it seemed like the kind of thing Dot would have circled.

He sends the workpaper and the chart to Priyanka, who reviews Vellacott's large loss files at Lime Street before anyone outside the building sees them. It's half past two there. She rings back at 10:15, his time, with a list. Your first chart. Which file, which version, what query? I can't re-perform it from this. He hadn't written it down. And page two says the amounts were chosen to avoid approval. You don't know that. You know they cluster under the line. She's right on both. He fixes them, writes her notes and his answers into the file, and feels, for the first time this week, that the work is better than he is.

Independent review by someone qualified, who didn't do the work, is how audit quality is assured. The reviewer checks whether the work can be re-performed and whether the evidence supports the words. Then the notes and how they were cleared go in the file.
Meridian's extract arrived through counsel at 10:40, with a cover letter, the query it was run with, and a one page control report printed from the settlement system.

Settlement system control report, March 2 to 5, 2027. Settlement records: 184,212. Total settled: $2,871,406,233.17. Extract run on March 11, 2027, at 2:02 in the afternoon UTC, by a read only reporting account.
Fourteen hundred UTC was seven that morning in Denver. A hundred and eighty four thousand rows, nearly three billion dollars, in four days. It was a big file, and he was about to build a lot on it.

His own count of the extract gives 184,212 rows and $2,871,406,233.17, to the cent. That ties it to Meridian's system. The independent half takes longer: a request through counsel for the Federal Reserve settlement totals for the same four days, due Monday. He writes both on the workpaper, the one done and the one waiting. Then he runs the first digits on all 184,212 rows. Apart from one lump, the curve falls away from 1 to 9 the way it should. The lump is the 2,906, and nothing else in four days.

Before relying on data, reconcile it to the source system's control totals and, where you can, to an independent record. The first shows the extract is complete as the system sees it. The second shows the system agrees with the outside world.
At 3:40 an email arrived from Marta Feld at Halverson Forensics, the firm Meridian had paid to validate the list.

An email from Marta Feld, Halverson Forensics. Subject: Our validation. Mr. Ashby, we understand you have questions about our review of the claimed settlements. Our team can walk you through our 25 item validation today at 5:30 PM at our 17th Street office. Our schedules are full after that until the week of March 22.
The science fair was at six, in Boulder, forty minutes away when the Turnpike behaved and an hour when it didn't.
He'd told Maisie on the phone he'd be there, and she'd made it the price of borrowing her project.

He asks for it another way: the population they sampled from, how the 25 were selected, what was checked on each, and the results, in writing, through counsel. He'd be glad of a call once he's read it. Marta Feld replies at 4:12 that she'll need to check with her client. That's an answer of its own. He finishes his notes, and at ten past five he's on the Turnpike with the sun low over the Flatirons.
To evaluate another party's sampling, get the population, the selection method, and the results, in writing. That's better evidence than a presentation, and it doesn't need a meeting at 5:30.

The gym at Maisie's school smelled of floor polish and hot glue, and it was full of trifold posters about volcanoes and plant growth and which paper towel was strongest. He got there at 5:52. Maisie saw him come in, looked away, and then looked back, which he decided to count.

Who Made These Up? had three charts now, the third with a new caption in black marker: Benford needs room. These bills only go from $61 to $148, so they cant spread out. Not broken! In the bottom corner, smaller: error found in a professional analysis using this method (12,401 should be 12,400). He didn't ask whose.
The judge was a retired engineer with a clipboard and reading glasses on a cord, and she asked exactly the question he'd hoped she would. Why doesn't your third chart work?

Maisie didn't look at him. It works fine, she said. The data just doesn't have room. Benford's for numbers that cover a lot of sizes. If everything's the same size, the first digits can't spread out. So if you see it fail, you have to ask if it should've worked in the first place. The judge wrote for a long time.
Laura came and stood next to him with two paper cups of lemonade and gave him one. She's been practicing that answer since Wednesday, she said. She wouldn't tell me who asked her the question.
She looked at the third chart. Those were my electric bills. Forty eight months, in a spreadsheet. She asked, I had them.
I'm finishing the PhD. Defense is April first. Don't make the joke. He didn't. That got him a funny look, over the rim of the cup.

Driving back down the Turnpike after nine, with Denver laid out ahead of him in orange lights, he went over the two days the way Dot would have, in order, with nothing improved. A tall bar that turned out to be 2,906 settlements and nothing else. A control report that only covered one date. A column of flags set by people with the keys to the table. A count that was wrong by one, found by his daughter, and fixed in the open. A reviewer in London who'd made the work better than he could on his own.
His phone buzzed at a red light on Speer.
A text from Nkechi Obi. How was the science fair?

He looked at it until the light changed. He hadn't told her about the science fair. He tried to remember whether he'd said it in front of Lou, or on the phone in the corridor at the Brown Palace, or anywhere at all, and couldn't. He typed Good, thanks, deleted it, and typed it again, and sent it, and then sat with the feeling that he'd just been asked a question by someone who already knew the answer.
At 10:15, back on Wazee Street, another one arrived.

A text from Lou. Inventory on her handbag came back. Reading glasses case, green pen, two more green pens, tea bags. And a State Capitol tour map, folded small. She'd circled the bit about the mile high step. In green. Copies tomorrow.
Henry opened his notebook to the page where he'd copied the sticky note on Tuesday. Check the year. Don't trust the dome.
The Capitol had a dome. It was gold, and it was on Broadway, and he'd walked past it most days for eleven months without once going up the steps.
